column1: The statement {{c1::CREATE TRIGGER}} defines a trigger and names its triggering events.
column2:
A trigger runs automatically when a specified event occurs.
Review source

column1: Triggers that respond to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements are {{c1::DML triggers}}.
column2:
DML means data manipulation language.
Review source

column1: Triggers that respond to schema events such as CREATE, ALTER, or DROP are {{c1::DDL triggers}}.
column2:
DDL means data definition language.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::AFTER INSERT}} to run trigger logic once an INSERT's actions and constraint checks succeed.
column2:
The trigger still runs within the firing transaction, not after COMMIT.
Review source

column1: To implement replacement UPDATE logic for a view, define an {{c1::INSTEAD OF UPDATE}} trigger.
column2:
The trigger can translate the requested view modification into changes to base tables.
Review source

column1: Inside an AFTER INSERT trigger, read new OrderID values with SELECT OrderID FROM {{c1::inserted}};
column2:
The logical table contains all rows added by that statement.
Review source

column1: Inside an AFTER DELETE trigger, read removed OrderID values with SELECT OrderID FROM {{c1::deleted}};
column2:
The logical table holds the rows as they existed before deletion.
Review source

column1: An UPDATE trigger sees old rows in deleted and new rows in {{c1::inserted}}.
column2:
The two logical tables expose the values before and after the update.
Review source

column1: One INSERT statement adding 100 rows directly invokes each matching INSERT trigger {{c1::once}}.
column2:
Triggers operate at statement level, so their logic must handle all affected rows together.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::set-based logic}} in DML triggers to process multiple affected rows instead of assuming a single row.
column2:
A cursor is not needed to process the inserted or deleted rowset.
Review source

column1: Compute total ordered quantity per product with SELECT ProductID, {{c1::SUM(Quantity)}} AS TotalQuantity FROM inserted GROUP BY ProductID;
column2:
An inventory trigger must subtract each product's total rather than one arbitrary inserted quantity.
Review source

column1: UPDATE(Price) identifies {{c1::an attempt to write Price}}, not proof that its value changed.
column2:
Even SET Price = Price can make the test pass.
Review source

column1: Detect nullable old/new price differences in SQL Server 2022 and later with oldPrice {{c1::IS DISTINCT FROM}} newPrice.
column2:
Unlike a simple inequality test, this detects transitions between NULL and a non-NULL value.
Review source

column1: A trigger can cover all three row-modification events with {{c1::AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE}}.
column2:
List the events with commas when one trigger must handle them together.
Review source

column1: Pair old and new UPDATE rows by joining inserted and deleted on an {{c1::unchanged, non-NULL unique key}}.
column2:
Row position is not a reliable way to match versions.
Review source

column1: To defer expensive processing, write event details to a {{c1::queue table}} for a separate job.
column2:
The trigger performs the small queue insert instead of the slow follow-up operation.
Review source

column1: A DML trigger and the statement that fires it participate in {{c1::the same transaction}}.
column2:
A trigger failure can affect the original modification, not just the trigger's own work.
Review source

column1: Raise a trigger validation error with {{c1::THROW}} 50001, 'Order date cannot be in the future', 1;
column2:
The unit uses this statement when inserted contains an invalid order date.
Review source

column1: The database option {{c1::RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS}} controls direct recursion of AFTER triggers.
column2:
This is a database-level option, not a complete guard against every trigger loop.
Review source

column1: RECURSIVE_TRIGGERS OFF blocks {{c1::direct recursion of AFTER triggers}}, not every trigger loop.
column2:
Indirect recursion needs separate controls and careful trigger design.
Review source

column1: At trigger entry, the BIGINT row-count test IF {{c1::ROWCOUNT_BIG() = 0}} RETURN; skips statements that affect no rows.
column2:
Make this test before any trigger statements that change the affected-row count.
Review source
